title: Three letters from the market, and a mast that leans

slides.heading: Three letters from one district, and a vowel that leans
body: Three consonants, and one district holds all three.
A vowel that leans forward over its letter.
And a vowel written with nothing at all.

slides.heading: Pen and paper
body: Real paper, a real pen.
Both halves of the name, out loud, every time.

slides.heading: The plate
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means a **plate**.
Mid class, in the market, with no new tone rule.

slides.heading: The cook who would not put it down
body: A noodle stall where the market aisle begins, and a cook with one trick.
The plate goes up on one finger and tilts as it slows.
A head at middle height, then a hook curving up and over.

slides.heading: The plate's letter
body: A head at middle height.
One hook curving up and over.

slides.heading: Write it
body: **Start at the head**, halfway up, clockwise.
Up, over, and down into the tail. One stroke.
Put it last in a syllable and it seals as a t-stop.

slides.heading: The turtle
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means a **turtle**.
A d and a t pressed flat, with no breath behind them.

slides.heading: The one nobody could keep in a basket
body: A shallow basket of turtles halfway down the aisle.
One of them pulled its head in until the shell dented.
**ด** keeps its rim round. **ต** carries the notch.

slides.heading: The turtle's letter
body: The same bowl as the child's letter.
A notch cut into the front of the rim.

slides.heading: Write it, and put it beside the child's letter
body: **Start at the head**, clockwise, round the bowl.
The notch goes into the rim on the way over.
Write **ด** beside it and compare the two rims.

slides.heading: The fish
body: Its name is the sound, then a word beginning with that sound.
The word means a **fish**.
A b and a p pressed flat, with the puff taken away.

slides.heading: The one that got out
body: Wide flat baskets, a hand's width of water, and one fish that goes.
Straight up, over the rim, and down on the boards.
**บ** stops level. **ป** carries one wall on up past the rim.

slides.heading: The fish's letter
body: The same bowl as the leaf's letter.
One wall rising clear past the rim.

slides.heading: Write it, and put it beside the leaf's letter
body: **Start at the head**, clockwise, round the bowl.
Carry the right stroke up past the rim and leave it standing.
Write **บ** beside it. Nothing else separates them.

slides.heading: Why the market is the district you can hear
body: Lesson three promised the missing puff would turn into a shortcut.
Palm up: **ก**, **ด**, **บ**, **จ**, **ต**, **ป**. Nothing lands on your hand.
A stop that releases no breath is mid class, with no way out of it.
Listen for the missing puff instead of memorising a list.

slides.prompt: Somebody hands you a Thai letter you have never seen and tells you only how it sounds: a plain stop with no breath behind it. Which district does it live in, and how sure are you allowed to be?

answers: Certain without seeing the shape, because the sound settles it.
Six of the market's nine letters are yours.

slides.heading: The third lodger on the front steps
body: The third lodger on the front steps.
One mast with its top curled into a forward lean.
Written ahead of the consonant, spoken after it.
Long and round, with the mouth held in one shape.

slides.heading: Write it
body: An upright with a loop curling forward at its head.
Write it ahead of the turtle's letter and say it aloud.
Consonant out of the mouth first, then the vowel.

slides.prompt: The leaning mast, the monkey's letter, the chicken sealing it. Out loud before you turn it over.

answers: Harbour letter, dead ending, long vowel. It falls.

slides.heading: And the short one
body: **โ-ะ** — the leaning mast in front, the two hooks behind.
The same shortener as lesson four, fourth time out.
Written out in full it needs a mark from a later lesson, so it waits for that.

slides.heading: What happens when a consonant follows it
body: A final consonant arrives and the hooks give way.
Nothing is written in their place at all.
Two bare consonants, and a short round vowel between them.

slides.prompt: The buffalo's letter, then the mouse's letter closing it. One beat. Out loud before you turn it over.

answers: The short round vowel sits between them, unwritten.

slides.heading: Two more built the same way
body: **ตก** — to fall.
**จน** — until.
One beat each, with the vowel supplied by you rather than by the page.

slides.prompt: You meet a two-letter word with no vowel written anywhere in it. What sound goes between the letters, and how many syllables is the word?

answers: The short round vowel of **โ-ะ**, with nothing on the page.
**One** syllable, opened and closed by the two letters.
The complete rule, and what three consonants do, comes later.

slides.prompt: Single mast, the fish's letter, the small roof, the mouse closing it. Watch the order. Out loud before you turn it over.

answers: **เป็น** — to be, and the tenth commonest word in Thai.
A lesson-seven vowel, a market letter, and the little roof.

slides.heading: Words these three letters open
body: **จะ** — marks the future, and the third commonest word in Thai.
**จาก** — from. **จับ** — to catch.
**ตา** — an eye. **ตาม** — to follow. **ตี** — to hit.
**ปาก** — a mouth. **ปี** — a year.
**โต** — to grow, or to be large. **โดย** — by, or by means of.

slides.heading: Twenty letters, and one corner of the grid still shut
body: Twenty letters, fifteen vowel spellings.
A market letter on a dead syllable is the one tone rule still missing.
Next: three vowels, a repeat mark, and two consonants run together.
